label: Chapter 7 · Part A
title: Common Objections I: “What Caused God?” and Other Misfires
tagline: Why the most popular objections miss the arguments they aim at
oneSentence: The best-known objections to First Cause arguments — “What caused God?”, “Maybe the universe is the uncaused cause”, “Why assume a beginning?”, “fallacy of composition”, “god of the gaps”, “a universe from nothing” — fail because they attack a caricature no major defender ever held, ignore the principled reasons the real arguments give, or quietly beg the question, so a serious critic has to engage the actual premises instead.
bigPicture:
After five proofs (chapters 1–5) and a long derivation of the divine attributes (chapter 6), Feser turns to the objections people actually raise. He has answered most of them already along the way, but he thinks a separate chapter is warranted for two reasons: there are some objections he has not yet addressed, and some of the weakest objections are so widespread — and so loudly repeated by the “New Atheist” writers (Dawkins, Dennett, Harris, Hitchens, Stenger, Krauss, Rosenberg, Grayling, Hawking and Mlodinow) — that they deserve a fresh, deeper look. This module covers the first half of that chapter: the objections aimed mainly at First Cause (cosmological) reasoning.

The unifying diagnosis is that almost every popular objection **misfires**: it is aimed at an argument nobody in the tradition ever gave. The flagship example is “If everything has a cause, then what caused God?” — an objection that presupposes the proofs start from the premise that *everything* has a cause, which none of them does. Feser devotes several pages to the history of this caricature, following the Thomist W. Norris Clarke in tracing it through Russell and the Mills back to Hume, who seems to have confused the rationalists’ talk of everything having a *sufficient reason* with the claim that everything has an *efficient cause distinct from itself*.

The remaining objections fall into recognizable families. Some nominate a rival stopping point (the universe, the Big Bang, the multiverse, quantum events, the laws of physics) while ignoring the criterion each proof uses to decide what can and cannot be a stopping point. Some deny that causal or explanatory principles hold universally, but rely on confusions (chance and indeterminism are not uncausedness) or on bad inferences (what we can *conceive* apart is not thereby *possible* apart). Some assume a temporal beginning or a linear series when the proofs concern a hierarchical, here-and-now series. Some misread technical terms — “necessary” as “true by definition”, “nothing” as a kind of exotic stuff. Some are true but irrelevant (the proofs don’t establish the Trinity). And the “god of the gaps” charge — which Feser calls the central conceit of the New Atheism — treats a metaphysical demonstration as if it were a rival scientific hypothesis.

This module matters enormously for the learner’s third goal, persuasion. In real conversations you will hear these objections far more often than any sophisticated criticism. Knowing *why* each one misfires, and being able to say so in a calm sentence or two, lets you redirect the conversation to where the genuine debate lies: whether the premises of the proofs — about act and potency, composition, essence and existence, and contingency — are true.
objectives: Explain the two independent reasons “If everything has a cause, what caused God?” fails: none of the proofs assumes everything has a cause, and each proof gives a principled reason why the First Cause could not have a cause.

Reconstruct W. Norris Clarke’s account of how the “everything has a cause” caricature entered the literature (Hume, the Mills, Russell, Hospers) through a confusion of efficient cause with sufficient reason.

Use each proof’s own criterion (potentiality, composition, essence–existence distinction, contingency) to show why the universe, Big Bang, multiverse, quantum events, or laws of physics cannot be the ultimate uncaused cause — and why the attempt would yield pantheism rather than atheism.
Distinguish chance and quantum indeterminism from uncausedness, and state three problems with Hume’s claim that we can conceive of an effect without a cause.
Explain why the proofs do not need a beginning of the universe, and why an endless stack of deeper physical laws would itself be a hierarchical series needing a first member.
Turn the fallacy-of-composition charge back on Hume and Grayling using the sticks, the mirrors, and Leibniz’s geometry books.
Distinguish logical, merely conditional, and metaphysical necessity, and use the distinction to rebut Kant’s and Grayling’s claim that the cosmological argument presupposes the ontological argument.
Explain why the proofs are not “god of the gaps” reasoning, and why Krauss’s and Hawking–Mlodinow’s “universe from nothing” never actually starts from nothing.
Give a calm, one-sentence reply to each objection and then redirect the conversation to the real premises.

summary.heading: Why a chapter on objections at all
summary.body: Most objections were already answered in earlier chapters, so Feser admits some overlap. A separate chapter is still warranted: some objections haven’t been addressed yet, and some very weak ones are so common — and so amplified by the New Atheist books of Harris, Dawkins, Dennett, Hitchens, Stenger, Hawking and Mlodinow, Krauss, Rosenberg, and Grayling — that they reveal pervasive misunderstanding and deserve a deeper look from new angles. Each section is headed by an objection in the critic’s own voice. This module covers the first run of them, aimed mainly at First Cause reasoning.

summary.heading: “If everything has a cause, what caused God?”
summary.body:
Perhaps the most common objection of all, raised by amateurs and professionals and repeated across New Atheist literature. Feser finds two independent flaws.

**A straw man.** None of the book’s arguments has “everything has a cause” as a premise, so charges of self-contradiction or arbitrary exception miss.

**The arguments explain why God has no cause.** Their point is to show there must be something that *could not* have a cause because it lacks the feature that makes other things need one:

- **Aristotelian:** potentials can’t actualize themselves; the purely actual has none to actualize.
- **Neo-Platonic:** composites need something to unite their parts; the absolutely simple has no parts.
- **Thomistic:** a thing’s essence must have existence joined to it; that whose essence *is* existence needs nothing joined.
- **Rationalist:** contingent things could have been otherwise; a necessary being could not.

(A footnote sets aside the Augustinian proof, which isn’t a causal argument.) Restated in these terms, the question asks what actualized the potentials of what has none, or what assembled the parts of what has none — questions without sense. Feser grants the atheist may doubt the arguments succeed or try to expose hidden incoherence in these notions. That is a real objection, and it requires grappling with details; a single smug question cannot replace it.

summary.heading: The straw man: the “basic cosmological argument”
summary.body:
The objection is popular because critics nearly always target a caricature. Feser’s examples span the spectrum: Dennett (New Atheist) says the argument’s simplest form is that everything has a cause, so the universe does; Nigel Warburton (popular introduction) says it traces a chain of prior causes back to a first one; Graham Priest (logician) motivates it with illnesses and car breakdowns having causes; Robin Le Poidevin (philosopher of religion) gives a three-step “basic cosmological argument” — whatever exists has a cause; nothing causes itself; the universe exists; so it has an external cause. Critics then ask what caused God, add that the argument assumes a beginning, and treat sophisticated versions as patches.

But not one major defender ever gave this argument — Feser lists some thirty, from Plato, Aristotle, Plotinus, Avicenna, Maimonides, Aquinas, Scotus, and Leibniz to Garrigou-Lagrange, Swinburne, Koons, Pruss, Oderberg, and Craig. Le Poidevin concedes that “no-one has defended a cosmological argument of precisely this form,” yet calls it a stepping-stone.

Feser’s analogy: suppose ID theorists defined basic Darwinism as a monkey giving birth to a human, admitted no one holds it, but called it a stepping-stone. Darwinians would rightly protest that it frames all their real claims as salvage work on an absurdity.

Nor are defenders implicitly committed to it: none uses “everything has a cause” (some deny it); none assumes a beginning (only the kalām version tries to prove one); most make no claim about the universe as a whole.

summary.heading: How the caricature spread: the Hume–Russell tradition
summary.body:
Critics learn about the argument from other critics, or read the caricature into Aquinas and Leibniz; repeated for generations, it became conventional wisdom even among specialists.

Feser follows W. Norris Clarke’s 1970 article on a “curious blind spot” in Anglo-American antitheism. Clarke found the caricature in mid-century textbooks, including John Hospers’ *An Introduction to Philosophical Analysis*, and suggested Russell’s *Why I Am Not a Christian* spread it; Russell got it from John Stuart Mill, who got it from James Mill; Hume’s *Dialogues* may be the first famous instance. Clarke notes that if anyone held “every being has a cause,” the refutation would be crushing — but its very ease should have raised suspicion, and no one in the tradition ever quotes a theist who holds it.

Hospers sneered that “many people” reach God by the argument and then forget it. Feser asks who they are, and turns the jibe around: the critics, having reached their preferred destination — dismissing Aristotle, Aquinas, and Leibniz wholesale — forget what those thinkers said. Clarke’s verdict: a tradition that misread its target at the start and has talked only to itself ever since.

summary.heading: Where the confusion began: two senses of “cause”
summary.body:
Clarke’s explanation of the origin: Hume misread Descartes and Spinoza. Descartes’ “preservation” argument in the Third Meditation implies that in some sense everything has a cause, but it still isn’t the straw man. It asks what keeps *Descartes* in existence, not what caused the universe; “everything has a cause” is not an explicit premise; and it makes no exception for God, whom Descartes calls self-caused.

What Descartes really means is close to the **principle of sufficient reason** (chapter 5): everything has an *explanation*. That differs from everything having a cause in the sense of an actualizer: all causes explain, but not all explanations are causes. PSR arguments make no exception for God — contingent things are explained by another, a necessary being by its own nature — so they contain no inconsistency.

Descartes and Spinoza blurred the two notions. Their word “cause” sounded like an **efficient cause distinct from its effect**, which God is said not to have. Hume fused the two claims and attributed the result to cosmological arguers generally, who indeed deny God has such a cause — hence the apparent contradiction. Clarke calls this target “a monster of their own fabrication,” a hybrid both Scholastics and Cartesians would reject. Hume had some excuse; his successors less. Feser treats assent to Clarke’s judgment as a test of competence and honesty, notes that Richard F. Clarke protested the same misrepresentation in 1889, and predicts the complaint will need repeating.

summary.heading: “Maybe the universe (or Big Bang, multiverse, quantum events, laws of physics) is the uncaused cause”
summary.body:
Found in Hume and in Dawkins, Dennett, Grayling, Krauss, Rosenberg, and Stenger, this also misses the point. The difference between God and everything else is principled, and the principle rules out these candidates:

- **Aristotelian:** the universe mixes act and potency; the Big Bang, each stage of a multiverse, and each quantum event (determinism aside) actualize potential; laws could have been otherwise, so are merely potential.
- **Neo-Platonic:** universe and multiverse are composite; laws and quantum events lack simplicity, their contingency revealing an essence–existence distinction.
- **Thomistic:** none has an essence identical with existence.
- **Rationalist:** all are contingent.

**Laws of nature** deserve special comment, their status being hotly disputed. If a law is a *statement of regularity*, it describes what needs explaining. If a *Platonic entity*, we must explain the world’s participation in it, and in these laws rather than others. If a *summary of how substances tend to behave* by nature (the Aristotelian view), it depends on those substances. On no view is it ultimate.

The atheist may reject these accounts, but merely *suggesting* the universe as terminus ignores the arguments. And success would yield **pantheism**, not atheism: a necessary, self-explanatory universe would be divine — acceptable to many Hindus, but not to Jews, Christians, Muslims, or atheists.

summary.heading: “Not everything has a cause”: chance and quantum mechanics
summary.body:
Stenger cites chance, Dennett and Rosenberg cite quantum mechanics, Grayling cites Hume. Even setting aside that the proofs don’t use “everything has a cause”, none of this touches the causal principles they do use.

**Chance** presupposes non-chance causes. A farmer striking buried treasure is chance, but only because two causal lines — his plowing, someone’s burying — intersect. A boulder shattering another after an earthquake is chance, but it rests on tectonics, gravity, and solidity. No defender ever denied chance.

**Quantum mechanics** shows at most that some events lack a *deterministic* cause, and neither causality nor PSR demands determinism. Moreover, quantum events occur only given contingent quantum laws, merely potential until a universe obeying them is actualized — so the appeal misses the point or begs the question.

summary.heading: The Humean objection: three problems
summary.body:
Grayling treats Hume’s claim that effects can be conceived apart from causes as decisive. Feser gives three reasons it isn’t.

1. **Special pleading.** No working scientist would accept that a phenomenon under study might have no cause; why accept it here? And, as Lloyd Gerson notes, the cosmological argument *is* an explanation, so “maybe there’s no explanation” gives no reason to reject it.
2. **Conceivability isn’t possibility.** One can conceive of a triangle without conceiving it as trilateral, or of a man without his height; neither could exist that way.
3. **Anscombe: underdescription.** What makes Hume’s imagined sudden appearance an *uncaused* coming-to-be rather than one with an unseen cause, or a teleportation? Settling that seems to require causation — e.g., distinguishing a generating from a transporting cause.

Earlier chapters treat these objections more fully.

summary.heading: “Why assume a beginning, or that the regress must end?”
summary.body:
Rosenberg and Krauss suggest a beginningless multiverse, with our Big Bang branching from a prior universe, removes the need for God; Krauss, citing Feynman, adds there might be endless deeper layers of physical law.

- The arguments don’t concern a beginning. Even a beginningless universe or multiverse would need a divine cause to sustain it and to explain why it exists at all.
- Laws cannot be ultimate explanations, however many layers.
- Stacked laws, each holding only as a special case of a deeper one, would form a **hierarchical series** of the chapter 1 kind, which must have a first member imparting causal power without deriving it. The New Atheists never address this.

summary.heading: “First Cause arguments commit a fallacy of composition”
summary.body:
The book’s arguments needn’t make any claim about the universe as a whole, and chapter 5 showed that the rationalist’s possible inference from contingent parts to a contingent whole isn’t fallacious.

Grayling, after Hume, says that once each member of a collection is explained, nothing is left over. Feser disagrees, recalling:

- **Sticks:** an infinite series of sticks, none able to move by itself individually or collectively, still needs an outside mover.
- **Mirrors:** an infinite row reflecting a face still needs a real face.
- **Leibniz’s geometry books:** endless copying from earlier copies never explains why the series has *this* content.

So Hume and Grayling commit the fallacy: explaining each member by its neighbor doesn’t explain why there is motion, an image, or geometrical content in the series at all.

summary.heading: “Even if there were a first cause, why think it is God?”
summary.body: Grayling, Dawkins, and Krauss assert there’s no reason to ascribe omnipotence, omniscience, or goodness to a first cause. Feser calls this as inept as “What caused God?” Defenders have given abundant arguments: Aquinas spends about a hundred double-column pages of the *Summa Theologiae* (right after the Five Ways) on simplicity, goodness, infinity, immutability, unity, knowledge, life, will, and power, and about two hundred pages of *Summa Contra Gentiles* book 1, with more in *De potentia* and *De veritate*; Samuel Clarke’s *Demonstration of the Being and Attributes of God* argues for infinity, omnipresence, unity, intelligence, free choice, power, wisdom, and goodness; Aristotle, Plotinus, Avicenna, Scotus, and Leibniz likewise. The New Atheists seem unaware of these arguments. And chapters 1–6 of this book argue for the attributes in detail. The objection is groundless.

summary.heading: “It wouldn’t prove prophets, the Bible, or the Trinity”
summary.body: True, but irrelevant. The arguments aim at one tenet shared by many religions — a cause of the world that is one, simple, immaterial, eternal, immutable, omnipotent, omniscient, and perfectly good. If they succeed, atheism is false and the open question is which theism to adopt (philosophical theism, Judaism, Christianity, Islam, or another), which needs further inquiry. Not answering every question about God is not answering none — as special relativity isn’t refuted by its silence on evolution, nor quantum mechanics by leaving engineering questions open.

summary.heading: “The cosmological argument presupposes the ontological argument”
summary.body:
Kant’s objection, repeated by Grayling, targets Descartes’ ontological argument (existence is a perfection, so a supremely perfect being must exist), on which God would exist *by definition*. Since the cosmological argument ends with a necessary being, Kant says it relies on that argument, which fails because existence is not a perfection.

**Reply.** Aquinas and most Thomists reject the ontological argument but defend the cosmological, so dependence can’t just be asserted. Nor are they inconsistent: as chapter 6 showed, the necessity they ascribe to God isn’t definitional, and Kant’s charge works only if it is.

**Grayling’s refinement.** A defender might call God *metaphysically* rather than *logically* necessary — a stopping point grounding contingent existence. But that, says Grayling, makes God merely a necessary *condition* of the world, not something that couldn’t fail to exist.

**Reply: a false dichotomy.** Metaphysical necessity can be unconditional without being logical. For the Aristotelian, contingency comes from mixing act and potency, so pure actuality exists necessarily. For the Neo-Platonist, it comes from composition, so the absolutely simple is necessary. For the Thomist, the first cause is necessary because its essence *is* existence, so nothing must be added to it. A footnote insists on “is” rather than “includes”, which would imply composition.

summary.heading: “God of the gaps”
summary.body:
The charge that God is invoked to fill a gap science has filled or will fill is, Feser says, the central conceit of the whole New Atheism: all genuine explanation is scientific, so God is at best a poor quasi-scientific hypothesis. Hitchens invokes Ockham’s razor; Dawkins thinks a Big Bang singularity or unknown physical concept more economical; Harris says nobody knows how the universe came to be; Krauss, Hawking, and Mlodinow think science has (nearly) explained it — Hawking and Mlodinow claiming that because of a law like gravity, “the universe can and will create itself from nothing.”

The **first** of two problems: this misses the point or begs the question.

- **Not gap-filling.** A god-of-the-gaps account allows that a natural explanation might in principle be correct and claims only greater probability. The book’s arguments are strict metaphysical demonstrations claiming no other explanation is possible in principle; they are not judged by parsimony or fit with current theory.
- **Metaphysical starting points.** They start from what any empirical theory presupposes: actualization of potential, composition, essence joined to existence, contingency. Insisting only science can explain assumes these arguments wrong without showing it.

summary.heading: A “universe from nothing”
summary.body:
The **second** problem: the proposed scientific explanation is a nonstarter, because a law like gravity isn’t nothing.

Krauss’s book notoriously commits the same error; Feser notes harsh criticism even from philosophers with no theological stake, especially David Albert’s 2012 *New York Times* review. Of about 185 pages, the first 152 argue the universe arose from empty space with energy under physical law — admitted not to be nothing. By about page 170 Krauss pares this to the laws of quantum gravity — also admitted not to be nothing. At page 177 he suggests layer upon layer of laws.

How any of this is “from nothing” is never explained. Talk of candidates for nothingness and of nothing as physical treats nothing as an elusive stuff that is hard to measure. But nothing is no stuff at all — simply the absence of anything. Krauss himself concedes his candidates aren’t really nothing, and what remains, laws or layers of laws, is something that can’t be the ultimate explanation.

(The chapter goes on to scientism, laws of nature, the complexity of a designer, and further objections, covered in ch7b.)
